summary.text: At \(n=140\), squaring rational bounds gives \(\lfloor140\sqrt{5/4}\rfloor=156\), \(\lfloor144\sqrt{5/4}\rfloor=160\), \(\lfloor157\sqrt{5/4}\rfloor=175\), and \(\lfloor161\sqrt{5/4}\rfloor=180\). Hence the four relevant terms are \(471,484,528,542\), but the claimed relation would require \(542=528+484-471=541\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\alpha=\sqrt{\frac54},\qquad f(k)=\lfloor k\alpha\rfloor,
\qquad q(k)=\left\lfloor\frac{k}{4}\right\rfloor.
\]
Thus the sequence is
\[
a(k)=2k+f(k)+q(k)\qquad(k\ge 1).
\]
We will show that the proposed recurrence fails at the valid index \(n=140\).

First, we record a way to evaluate the needed irrational floors using only integer arithmetic. If nonnegative integers \(k,m\) satisfy
\[
4m^2\le 5k^2<4(m+1)^2,
\]
then
\[
f(k)=\left\lfloor k\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=m.
\]
Indeed, put \(x=k\sqrt{5/4}\). Then \(x\ge0\), and
\[
x^2=k^2\frac54.
\]
Dividing the displayed integer inequalities by \(4\) gives
\[
m^2\le x^2<(m+1)^2.
\]
All of \(m,x,m+1\) are nonnegative, so comparison of their squares yields
\[
m\le x<m+1.
\]
This is exactly the condition that \(\lfloor x\rfloor=m\).

We now apply this observation at the four indices occurring in the recurrence when \(n=140\). The necessary exact inequalities are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
k&m&4m^2&5k^2&4(m+1)^2\\ \hline
140&156&97344&98000&98596\\
144&160&102400&103680&103684\\
157&175&122500&123245&123904\\
161&180&129600&129605&131044
\end{array}
\]
In every row the middle entry lies between the entries on its left and right, with the right-hand inequality strict. Consequently,
\[
f(140)=156,\qquad f(144)=160,\qquad
f(157)=175,\qquad f(161)=180.
\]

For completeness, the other floor term causes no discrepancy in this recurrence. In fact, for every nonnegative integer \(n\),
\[
q(n+21)+q(n)=q(n+17)+q(n+4).
\]
To see this, write \(n=4t+r\), where \(0\le r<4\). Then \(q(n)=t\) and \(q(n+4)=t+1\). If \(r=0,1,2\), then
\[
q(n+17)=t+4,\qquad q(n+21)=t+5,
\]
whereas if \(r=3\), then
\[
q(n+17)=t+5,\qquad q(n+21)=t+6.
\]
In either case, \(q(n+21)-q(n+17)=1=q(n+4)-q(n)\), proving the identity. The linear terms also cancel because
\[
2(n+21)+2n=2(n+17)+2(n+4).
\]
Therefore the proposed recurrence, written without subtraction as
\[
a(n+21)+a(n)=a(n+17)+a(n+4),
\]
would at any index be equivalent to
\[
f(n+21)+f(n)=f(n+17)+f(n+4).
\]
At \(n=140\), however, the floor values just established give
\[
f(161)+f(140)=180+156=336,
\]
while
\[
f(157)+f(144)=175+160=335.
\]
Thus the two sides differ by \(1\).

Equivalently, one can evaluate the four sequence terms themselves. Since
\[
q(140)=35,\quad q(144)=36,\quad q(157)=39,\quad q(161)=40,
\]
we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(140)&=2\cdot140+156+35=471,\\
a(144)&=2\cdot144+160+36=484,\\
a(157)&=2\cdot157+175+39=528,\\
a(161)&=2\cdot161+180+40=542.
\end{aligned}
\]
The conjectured recurrence at \(n=140\) asserts
\[
a(161)=a(157)+a(144)-a(140).
\]
Its right-hand side is
\[
528+484-471=541,
\]
whereas its left-hand side is \(542\). Hence the asserted equality is false at \(n=140\). Since \(140\ge1\), this is an admissible index, and a single such counterexample disproves the universal conjecture.
